about: Every CS Quest slide picture, keyed. A slide names a key (img); the picture lives at public/img/<key>.webp (1280x720 WebP; a picture a slide crops very narrow is captured at 2x, 2560x1440, the same layout). Decks and this manifest are checked by `npm run csq:check`; captures are made by scripts/csq-shots.js.

images.concept: Say only what it shows: a chart does not say why
images.alt: The claim card beside the plant chart: each claim must match what the bars actually show, nothing more.

images.concept: Is it true? A claim is backed up by evidence
images.alt: The Plant Race case: a chart of a growing plant, and claim cards waiting to be judged against it.

images.concept: Predict the plant: it grows 2 cm every day
images.alt: Predict Day 6: the plant chart climbs the same amount every day, so the next bar can be predicted from the pattern.

images.concept: Enough data? Two bars are a hunch, not a case
images.alt: The Two Points case: a chart with almost no data in it, where the honest answer is that we cannot tell yet.

images.concept: Clean it first: fix typos, merge repeats, remove impossible values
images.alt: Double Trouble: a second messy case, where the same student answered twice and one row must go.

images.concept: Real data is messy: typos, repeats and impossible numbers
images.alt: The Twelve Pets case as it arrived: a messy table where one kind of pet hides under several spellings.

images.concept: Compare by percent: part divided by whole, times 100
images.alt: Tidy, Then Compare: two cleaned sets side by side, the case where comparing fairly means comparing percents.

images.concept: Pet survey clean-up: three spellings of dog split one bar into three
images.alt: The cleaned pet chart: the three misspelled dogs are fixed to one spelling, and the Dog bar counts all seven.

images.concept: Fix the question: let every answer feel equally welcome
images.alt: One Grade Asked: a fairness case about who a survey asked, and who it never reached.

images.concept: A bigger, fairer sample: more answers from more kinds of people
images.alt: Who Is Missing? The fairness case that asks which people a sample left out before trusting its answer.

images.concept: Rules that predict: a model is a rule, a simulation runs it
images.alt: The Ramp Rule case: a rule that predicts how far a car rolls, with the ramp and the trials waiting.

images.concept: The ramp: every trial went farther than predicted, so refine the rule
images.alt: The ramp trials ran farther than the first rule predicted, so the rule was raised and run again: the error shrinks.

images.concept: Predict, compare, refine: change the model, not the data
images.alt: The model has run: predicted distances sit beside the real trials, so the rule can be compared and refined.

images.concept: One trial is not proof: compare the model with many results
images.alt: Bounce Back: another model case with its own trials, because one lucky trial never proves a rule.

images.concept: From tally to chart: one bar per answer, the tallest jumps out
images.alt: The survey tallies turned into a bar chart: one bar per pet, and the dog bar towers over the rest.

images.concept: Data from real people: today the data comes from people around you
images.alt: My Data opens a class survey: one question, and answer rows waiting for the class to fill them in.

images.concept: Ask someone else: another pair of eyes may see what you missed
images.alt: A second survey question waits in My Data: fresh answers to collect before anyone pins a claim about them.

images.concept: Tally marks: each answer gets one mark, counted in fives
images.alt: Tallying the survey: answers are counted with the steppers, each one adding to its row of the class data.

images.concept: Fair questions first: answers can only be fair if questions are fair
images.alt: My Data in Pro: a survey question and its answer rows, where fairness starts with how the question is asked.

images.concept: Compare by percent: compare 72% with 50%, not 18 with 20
images.alt: A third survey question in My Data: the case for comparing classes by percent instead of raw counts.

images.concept: Leading questions: a question that pushes builds in bias
images.alt: A second Pro survey question: its wording matters, because a pushing question bends the data before counting.

images.concept: Show me first: pin a claim only when the view on screen shows it
images.alt: With the grouped chart showing the evidence, the claim card opens: Dot will only pin a claim the view proves.

images.concept: Sort or group: grouping puts the same kind together and counts them
images.alt: The pet case grouped: one bar per kind of pet, counted, so the most common pet jumps out of the chart.

images.concept: Meet Dot: a detective solves cases with facts, not guesses
images.alt: Dot opens the first case: a table of who, where and when facts in rows and columns, and the question: who was last in the hall?

images.concept: Data is facts in rows: a table holds facts in rows and columns
images.alt: Another case table: every row is one tower of blocks, every column one kind of fact about it.

images.concept: Who was in the lunchroom last? Sort by the column the question asks about
images.alt: The case sorted by time: the Hall rows now run in time order, so the last Hall row answers the question.

images.alt: Escape the Post Office: six trick locks guard the sorting room door, one for each Defender stamp.

images.concept: the inbox lock

images.concept: a prize you never entered
images.alt: Lock 4, message 2 of 6: a Prize Parrot says you won a shiny prize you never tried to win. Tap fast!

images.concept: a wobble, not a fail

images.concept: the inbox lock (Pro)
images.alt: Lock 4 at Pro: the first of eight messages, with four moves to choose from and a hint feather below.

images.concept: a spoofed sender in the lock
images.alt: Lock 4 at Pro, message 5 of 8: Post Office asks you to confirm your key, but the postmark is a far-town hand stamp.

images.concept: the layers lock
images.alt: Lock 6, Layers: a snooper tries to peek inside a sealed note. Four layers wait: padlock, key checker, patch crew, copy vault.

images.concept: a guesser at the mailbox
images.alt: Threat 2 of 4: a guesser tries key after key on a mailbox. Which layer stops it?

images.concept: a known hole
images.alt: Threat 3 of 4: an old lock has a known hole that anyone can use. The Patch Crew waits among the layers.

images.concept: the only copy
images.alt: Threat 4 of 4: a flood soaks the only copy of a letter. The Copy Vault keeps a spare somewhere else.

images.concept: defense in depth
images.alt: Lock 6 at Pro: an interceptor reads a note while it travels. Six layers wait, from padlock to long passphrase.

images.concept: a stolen key
images.alt: Threat 2 of 6: a stolen key is tried on the mailbox from a new device. The Key Checker is one of six layers.

images.concept: a known hole (Pro)
images.alt: Threat 3 of 6: a known hole in old software lets a trick letter slip in. The Patch Crew closes it.

images.concept: six layers
images.alt: Threat 5 of 6: a faked postmark fools the front desk. All six layers are on the table.

images.concept: a guessed key
images.alt: Threat 6 of 6: a one-word key is guessed in an afternoon. The Long Passphrase layer stops it.

images.concept: the five moves
images.alt: Lock 5, Five Moves: a message unkind to Sam is going around the class chat. Five move tiles wait to be put in order.

images.concept: four moves placed
images.alt: Four moves in order: Stop, Save it, Tell a trusted adult, Block or report. Carry on is the last tile.

images.concept: stop, then save
images.alt: Two moves placed in order: Stop, do not pass it on, then Save it, keep the message.

images.concept: the incident drill
images.alt: Lock 5 at Pro: someone has a classmate's mailbox key, and a second message pressures you. Six drill tiles wait.

images.concept: the drill, done
images.alt: Lock 5 open: the drill ran in order, start to finish. Calm work, and the skill it trained.

images.concept: report and recover
images.alt: Five drill moves in order, up to change the key from a clean device. Only the one-line log is left.

images.concept: contain first
images.alt: The drill begins: Stop and disconnect is placed first. Five tiles still wait to be put in order.

images.concept: preserve and tell
images.alt: Three drill moves in order: stop and disconnect, save the evidence, tell a trusted adult, fast.

images.concept: the sealed note
images.alt: Lock 2, Sealed Note: the Magpie's note reads RSHQ, and the cipher wheel turns it back one step at a time.

images.concept: the sealed note, read
images.alt: Lock 2 turned to shift 3: the Magpie's note RSHQ now reads OPEN, and the lock is ready to open.

images.concept: the sealed note (Pro)
images.alt: Lock 2 at Pro: the Magpie's sealed note waits beside the cipher wheel. No first letter is given this time.

images.concept: which Pim is real
images.alt: Lock 3, Which Pim?: three cards say they are from Pim. Each lists a postmark, a footprint and what it asks for.

images.concept: the real Pim, picked
images.alt: The real Pim is picked: a Netville postmark, owl footprints, and a request for help in the open.

images.concept: which Pim is real (Pro)
images.alt: Lock 3 at Pro: three cards from Pim. One postmark is stamped by a hand press, and one asks for a secret.

images.concept: the real Pim, picked (Pro)
images.alt: The real Pim is picked at Pro: the office stamp, the worn left-edge footprint, help asked in the open.

images.concept: Make the number 5: turn on the switches that add up to 5
images.alt: The 4 card and the 1 card are switched on: 4 and 1 make 5, the number this round asked for.

images.concept: On or off: everything inside is tiny switches, called bits
images.alt: Five bit switches, all off, with their cards: 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. One switch on adds its card.

images.concept: Where does a photo live? In storage, as bits, even when off
images.alt: The photo question: where is a photo when the tablet is off? The answer the game teaches is storage, as bits.

images.concept: Counting with bits: read the cards whose switch is on
images.alt: A reading round: some switches are already on, and the question is what number their cards add up to.

images.concept: Pictures are dots: a picture is tiny dots called pixels
images.alt: The pixel grid: a picture drawn one dot at a time, each cell lit or dark like a bit.

images.concept: More bits, more values: eight bits, a byte, show 256 grays
images.alt: Eight switches in a row: a full byte, worth 0 to 255. Only the 128 switch is on, making the middle gray.

images.concept: One thing, many codes: 21 in decimal is 10101 in binary
images.alt: The switches read 16, 4 and 1 switched on: the number 21 written in bits instead of decimal.

images.concept: Everything is numbers: letters and colors are bits too
images.alt: Pro bits opens with five switches and a bigger ask: make 21, where every place is worth double the last.

images.concept: Binary place values: each place is worth double the one to its right
images.alt: The color round: a swatch to match with three numbers, because a pixel mixes red, green and blue light.

images.concept: Every switch is for someone: captions, read-aloud, text size, contrast
images.alt: The audit round: a real game is checked setting by setting — captions, text size, contrast — for who each helps.

images.concept: Made for everyone: a good game works for people who differ
images.alt: Design Lab opens with a user to design for: their needs come first, before any setting is touched.

images.concept: Help one, help many: captions help in a noisy room too
images.alt: A second Design Lab user: a change made for one person usually turns out to help many more.

images.concept: Bias: tech works worse for some when testers were all alike
images.alt: A Pro brief about bias: when a product fails some people, the testing group is the first place to look.

images.concept: Edges help everyone: contrast for low vision helps in bright sun too
images.alt: A Pro brief about designing at the edges: a mode made for low vision is the mode everyone uses in sun.

images.concept: Design for real people: start with how real people use a thing
images.alt: Design Lab in Pro opens with a real user and their words: design starts from what people actually say.

images.concept: Who was missing? Find the gap in the testing group, then widen it
images.alt: The last Pro brief: find who was missing from the testers, then widen the group until nobody is.

images.concept: Quick checks first: on, plugged in, muted — restart comes later
images.alt: A second ticket waits at the desk: the quick, cheap checks are the ones a good fixer tries first.

images.concept: Small clues: caps lock, a frozen app — the clue points at the fix
images.alt: A fourth ticket with a small clue in its story: reading the clue closely points straight at the fix.

images.concept: It is not working! Good fixers have a plan, not a panic
images.alt: The Fix-It Desk opens its first ticket: a broken gadget, its story, and the fix options with their minutes.

images.concept: No sound: troubleshooting is a checklist, not a guess
images.alt: The No Sound ticket: the headphones fix is under way, with plugged in and volume checked on the list.

images.concept: One change at a time: change one thing, then test again
images.alt: A second Pro ticket: the flowchart way means one change, one test, and knowing what fixed it.

images.concept: Fixers do not guess: a flowchart of yes/no questions, cheapest first
images.alt: The Pro Fix-It Desk opens a flow ticket: the fix is a chain of yes and no questions, cheapest first.

images.concept: The swap test: swap in a part you know works and watch the problem
images.alt: A later Pro ticket: the kind where swapping in a known-good part tells you where the fault lives.

images.concept: The printer prints nothing: cheap checks before slow, expensive ones
images.alt: A third Pro ticket at the desk: its story hides the clue, and the cheap checks come before the slow ones.

images.concept: A step counter: small, cheap, lasts all day — pick only what it needs
images.alt: The Step counter brief: a shoe clip that counts steps, small, cheap and lasting all day, with cost, battery and size meters.

images.concept: Sensors: a sensor measures the world — light, motion, sound
images.alt: A second gadget brief: choosing parts starts with the sensor that measures what the gadget must notice.

images.concept: What makes a gadget: sensors, a processor, outputs, a connection and power
images.alt: A Noise meter brief: it must hear the room, show the loudness, send a log to the laptop and run on wall power.

images.concept: Tradeoffs: every part costs money, battery and space
images.alt: A third brief with tighter limits: every part added moves the cost, battery and size meters.

images.concept: Every task needs both: a photo needs the camera and the camera app
images.alt: An ordering round: the steps of one task laid out, where hardware and software take turns doing the work.

images.concept: Hardware and software: hardware you can touch, software is instructions
images.alt: The hardware and software sort: cards for screens and apps wait to be split into touchable and instructions.

images.concept: Every part has a job: inputs, outputs, processor, storage, battery
images.alt: Inside the machine: the cutaway view where the processor, storage and battery do their jobs together.

images.concept: Meet Gizmo: every device is a team of parts
images.alt: Gizmo opens the tablet: its parts are laid out as a team, and the first job asks which part does it.

images.concept: A tap travels: finger, touch sensor, processor, the app, screen
images.alt: The controller pad wiring round: parts are joined in the order a signal travels from input to output.

images.concept: a note anyone can read
images.alt: A note to send: OAK TREE, readable by anyone. Three scrambled readings wait below; only one uses the shift of 5.

images.concept: a secret word, shift unknown
images.alt: A secret word, DAOWQF, with no shift marked on the card. Only trying the wheel will show what it says.

images.concept: Secret codes for fun: a cipher wheel shifts each letter by the key (shift 3)
images.alt: The cipher wheel: turn the key and every letter shifts, turning a plain message into a secret one.

images.concept: Brute force: a shift has only 25 keys, so you can try them all
images.alt: A later cipher level: with so few keys, trying every one is a real way in — for a shift cipher.

images.concept: crack it by counting letters
images.alt: Crack it by counting: a scrambled message, the Caesar wheel, and a button that counts how often letters appear.

images.concept: Hiding is not scrambling: steganography hides a message in a picture's pixels
images.alt: Steganography: a heart hidden in a picture. Each pixel is a number, and its last bit says dot or blank, so the picture looks the same.

images.concept: Scramble it: encryption makes a message unreadable without the key
images.alt: Secret Messages in Pro: the cipher wheel waits with a scrambled message only the key can open.

images.concept: the two-key lockbox card
images.alt: The two-key lockbox card: anyone can click it shut, but only the owner holds the key that opens it.

images.concept: A shift of 3: every letter moves the same number of places
images.alt: The wheel at work: letters are shifting along the alphabet by the key, turning plain words into code.

images.concept: the title screen
images.alt: Packet Post's title screen: Pim the owl at the Netville post office. Deliver every packet. Keep every secret.

images.concept: Keep a spare copy: a backup kept somewhere else
images.alt: A Good Spare Copy: the sorting round that tells a real backup, kept somewhere else, from a copy that is not.

images.concept: Build a passphrase: four random words, long and hard to guess
images.alt: The passphrase is taking shape: words are being picked for the mailbox key, and longer means harder to guess.

images.concept: one key for every door
images.alt: If one key opens every door, losing it opens them all: a habit card waits to be sorted, safe or risky.

images.concept: Lock it up: lock it, keep the key, keep a spare copy
images.alt: The mailbox key builder: pick words for a passphrase, the key that locks your mailbox in Packet Post.

images.concept: habits that protect a tablet
images.alt: A tablet holds messages and pictures. Signing out on a shared computer: does the habit protect it, or is it risky?

images.concept: Private or fine to share? Some things stay private
images.alt: The sharing sort: cards to split into Share and Keep Private, from favorite animals to passphrases.

images.concept: Who may know it? Only a trusted adult may know your passphrase
images.alt: Okay to Tell: a sorting round about who may hear what, where a passphrase is never fine to share.

images.concept: the backup rule in four steps
images.alt: The backup rule in four steps: make a second copy, keep it in another place, check it opens, keep it fresh.

images.concept: Two halves of security: physical protects the machine, digital the data
images.alt: Lock It in Pro opens with the sharing sort: security starts with knowing what must be protected.

images.concept: Strong passphrases: four random words beat a short word plus a number
images.alt: The Pro mailbox key builder: a passphrase made of chosen words, different from every other account key.

images.concept: Think before you post: making something public has a benefit and a risk
images.alt: The last Lock It sort in Pro: judging what is safe to do, the habit of naming a risk before you act.

images.concept: build a new key from word tiles
images.alt: The home router still has its key on a sticker anyone can read. Build a new passphrase from four word tiles.

images.concept: The padlock: details travel sealed, like an envelope, not a postcard
images.alt: The sealed route: a message travels a road marked sealed, the padlock idea played as a journey.

images.concept: Physical or digital? Sort each measure by what it protects
images.alt: Physical or Digital: the sort whose bins are the machine and the data, from locked doors to firewalls.

images.concept: every road meets at the center office
images.alt: Five packets for the zoo: every road on this map meets at the center office, where many hands can carry them.

images.concept: Meet Pim: every message must reach the right house
images.alt: Pim opens the Netville map: houses, roads and the first message waiting to be delivered.

images.concept: Back in order: numbers put arriving packets back together
images.alt: Packets are on the roads of Netville, each carrying its number, so the far end can rebuild the message in order.

images.concept: Too big to send: the network cuts a message into numbered packets
images.alt: Break It Up: a message too big for one trip is cut into small numbered packets at the post office.

images.concept: say got it, the first round
images.alt: Say Got It begins: three packets are on the road to the mill office, and the second one has fallen off the van.

images.concept: Say got it: the receiver confirms each packet and asks for missing ones
images.alt: The delivery is under way: packets have been sent and the receiver is saying got it, watching for a gap.

images.concept: Damaged on the way? A checksum count that does not match means resend
images.alt: A later protocol level on the road: here a damaged packet must be spotted by its count and sent again.

images.concept: design the rule set
images.alt: Design the rule set: three things go wrong on this road, and four rule cards are there to catch them.

images.concept: Messages in packets: numbered, routed and rebuilt at the other end
images.alt: Rules of the Road opens: numbered packets wait at the first router, ready to travel by the shared rules.

images.concept: Rules everyone follows: a protocol is rules every computer agrees on
images.alt: A second protocol level: every router on the road follows the same rules, or no packet could be passed on.

images.concept: a packet on its journey
images.alt: The second of four packets is on its way across the diamond map, two hops done and two to go.

images.concept: Many roads: each packet can take a different road through routers
images.alt: Many Roads: the town map offers more than one road between the same houses, and a closed road is not the end.

images.concept: Hops: each jump between routers is one hop, inside a hop budget
images.alt: Many Roads in Pro: the map counts hops, and a busy router means picking another path inside the budget.

images.concept: sealed roads wear padlocks
images.alt: Sealed roads wear padlocks: open roads cost one hop, but a snoopy cat reads every packet on them.

images.concept: Trick or safe? A threat, a rush and a key request
images.alt: A second message card to judge: is it a trick with clues, or a safe message with none?

images.concept: Clues of a trick: hurry, a prize, a request for your passphrase
images.alt: Checking the message: the first clue is marked, and the card still has more of its tricks to find.

images.concept: Some messages are tricks: they want you to hurry or give things away
images.alt: Spot the Trick opens its first message card: friendly words on the surface, and clues hiding in the text.

images.concept: What to do: do not reply, do not tap, tell a trusted adult
images.alt: Card 3 of 6 is safe: a field trip note from your teacher, a known sender who asks for nothing.

images.concept: a stranger asks for your street
images.alt: A trick card from someone you do not know: it fishes for the street a player lives on.

images.concept: a trick wearing a bank's name
images.alt: A trick wearing a bank's name: for your safety, it says, confirm your mailbox key and your birthday.

images.concept: Faked senders: a trick can fake its sender name, called spoofing
images.alt: A Pro trick card: the sender name looks friendly, but a faked name is exactly what spoofing means.

images.concept: a parcel you never ordered
images.alt: A parcel trick: a delivery you never ordered is waiting, and a small fee must be paid within two hours.

images.concept: Bolt in the fog
images.alt: Fog covers Bolt's board: only the squares near Bolt can be seen, so no fixed list of steps could work here.

images.concept: Worked example: the fog-proof program
images.alt: The repeat until goal program with the if / else inside it, feeling its way along the dry path across a board of water.

images.concept: If, else: two ways
images.alt: One if / else block in the tray: if path ahead, move; else, turn left. Bolt checks and picks a side every time it runs.

images.concept: When: things that happen
images.alt: A when block waits at the top of the program: when a gem is picked up, turn right, with the driving loop underneath it.

images.concept: Two questions at once: AND
images.alt: A two-question check in the tray: if wall ahead AND on a gem, pick up and turn; the spiral maze waits on the board.

images.concept: Worked example: one program, any maze
images.alt: The short sense-and-steer program beside the maze: repeat until goal, if path ahead move, else turn right.

images.concept: Decide at every step
images.alt: The maze program checks at every step: repeat until goal, if path ahead move, else turn left, on a water board.

images.concept: Mission board: the big maze start
images.alt: A big walled maze with Bolt penned in one corner and the flag far away: no fixed route can be written for this.

images.concept: OR and NOT
images.alt: The check reads if NOT path ahead OR on paint, turn right: one block asking two questions at once.

images.concept: When meets if
images.alt: The Pro event program: a when block for picking up a gem, over a repeat loop whose if block picks up gems Bolt stands on.

images.concept: One too many: a repeat count one too big is a common bug
images.alt: The broken program is one repeat block set to 6, but the flag is five squares away: one move too many.

images.concept: Done means tested: a fix is done when you run it again
images.alt: The fixed program sits in the tray: the wrong turn left has become turn right, ready to run again and be tested.

images.concept: Programs break: a bug is a mistake in a program
images.alt: The Debug Lab opens a program that does not work: Bolt waits at the start while the broken program fills the tray.

images.concept: Expected and actual: compare what Bolt did with what you expected
images.alt: Bolt has run part of the broken program and stopped in the wrong place: what Bolt did is not what the program promised.

images.concept: Step, stop, fix: step one block at a time and stop at the first surprise
images.alt: Stepping one block at a time: the first block is lit in the tray and Bolt has moved exactly one square.

images.concept: Edge cases: unusual boards break quiet assumptions
images.alt: A later Debug Lab board with an unusual layout: goals and walls sit where a program that assumes too much will fail.

images.concept: Expect bugs: a test case is one board with a known right answer
images.alt: A Pro Debug Lab board with its test tabs above it: one program must pass every board, not just this one.

images.concept: One board can hide a bug: the same program on a second test board
images.alt: The same program on Test 3, a longer hallway: Test 1 and Test 2 show a check, Test 3 a cross, and Bolt splashed into the water.

images.concept: The debug loop: a fix is done only when every test passes
images.alt: After a run, every test tab shows a mark: Test 1 and Test 2 pass, Test 3 fails, so this fix is not done yet.

images.concept: Defined is not called
images.alt: The My Block named Side is defined in the tray, but nothing calls it, and Bolt has not moved: a definition alone does nothing.

images.concept: Stairs, stairs, stairs
images.alt: Three gem steps climb like stairs to the flag, and Bolt's program tray is empty: climbing all three the long way takes a lot of blocks.

images.concept: Make your own block
images.alt: The My Block named Stair is built in the tray: move, pick up, turn right, move, turn left: one named packet of blocks.

images.concept: Notes and credit
images.alt: Two My Blocks named Zig sit in the tray, and the second carries a based-on Starter blocks stamp: a remix keeps its credit.

images.concept: Call it three times
images.alt: The Stair block is defined once, then called three times in a row at the bottom of the tray: call Stair, call Stair, call Stair.

images.concept: Blocks built by others
images.alt: The team's My Block Zigzag (n) heads the program, with its note: By the Robo Route team. It climbs the zigzag staircase on the board.

images.concept: Notes and credit (Pro)
images.alt: Three My Blocks carry plain-language notes: Sweep picks up the gems, Drop drives down the side, Home drives to the goal.

images.concept: A block with a number slot
images.alt: My Block Dash (n) repeats n moves, and the calls underneath feed it different numbers: call Dash (7), (6), (5), (4), (3).

images.concept: One block per job
images.alt: Three named My Blocks split the job: GetGems, Climb and Cross, each defined in the tray and called in turn below.

images.concept: Worked example: three rooms, one block
images.alt: Room (steps) is defined once with steps inside it, then called three ways: call Room (1), call Room (3), call Room (2).

images.concept: Loops save work
images.alt: Five separate move blocks stacked in the tray do the same job as one repeat block, but take five times the room.

images.concept: The repeat bracket
images.alt: One bracket does the work: a repeat 5 times block with a single move block inside it, and Bolt's row of five squares ahead.

images.concept: The number matters
images.alt: A repeat 2 times bracket holds move, move, pick up, and one more move follows it: Bolt drives five squares and picks up both gems.

images.concept: Any block can go inside
images.alt: The repeat bracket holds turn right instead of move, so Bolt would spin on one square instead of driving anywhere.

images.concept: Loops save work (Pro board)
images.alt: A repeat 7 times block with one move inside crosses Bolt's whole row; written out longhand it would take seven blocks.

images.concept: A loop inside a loop
images.alt: A repeat 3 times bracket holds a second repeat 3 times bracket with move inside it, then turn right: a loop in a loop.

images.concept: Predict the count
images.alt: A nested repeat program next to a staircase of gems: repeat 3 times outside, repeat 2 times with move and pick up inside.

images.concept: Nested loops climb stairs
images.alt: The nested-loop program beside a walled staircase board: the inner repeat climbs, the turn starts the next step up.

images.concept: The maker loop: Check proves a level can be solved and shows its par
images.alt: A level built in the maker: Bolt, a gem, a key, a door and the goal on the board, and Check says it can be solved: par 17.

images.concept: Be the game designer: plan, build, test, fix, explain
images.alt: The Level Maker's first task: the goal is walled in, and the floor and wall tools wait beside the board.

images.concept: Plan it first: start, goal and one tricky part
images.alt: A second maker task brief on the canvas: each task says what the level must contain before a single square is painted.

images.concept: The designer stays quiet: a tester plays while the designer watches
images.alt: The built level handed to a tester: the tester builds a program and Bolt drives it, while the maker watches without helping.

images.concept: Iterate: plan, build, Check, test, change, test again
images.alt: A Pro maker level with a gem, a key and a door on the way to the goal, and Check says it can be solved: par 23.

images.concept: Feedback is information: it shows where a player got stuck
images.alt: After a friend tests the level, the tester card asks for one fun thing and one confusing thing, with nothing to type.

images.concept: Design for someone else: plan, build, test, improve, document
images.alt: The Pro Level Maker's first task: the goal is walled in, and the tools to open the walls wait beside the board.

images.concept: Keep a timeline: split the work and set times
images.alt: A second Pro maker task: the brief sets what to build, the way a team plan sets who does each part and by when.

images.concept: Pick the better route
images.alt: The compare screen: Route A takes 7 blocks with one turn, Route B takes 8 blocks with two turns, and a green Use button sits in each panel.

images.concept: Meet Bolt: a program is a list of steps
images.alt: Bolt the robot at the start of a short dotted path, with the goal flag four squares ahead and an empty program tray.

images.concept: Steps run in order, first to last
images.alt: Bolt's program tray holds four move blocks stacked in order, matching the four dotted squares between Bolt and the flag.

images.concept: A turn spins Bolt in its square
images.alt: Bolt has driven four squares, then turned left in the same square to face the flag; the turn block is lit in the tray.

images.concept: Worked example: turn right, move, move
images.alt: Bolt at the top left, facing along the top row, the flag at the bottom, and a program: turn right, four moves, turn left, three moves.

images.concept: Compare routes
images.alt: A walled maze with two ways around the walls to the flag, one shorter than the other.

images.concept: Plan before you build
images.alt: Bolt on a longer open board with the flag far to the right: too many squares to cross one careless step at a time.

images.concept: A plan is the steps in plain words
images.alt: A plan card lists three plain-language plan lines for the level, waiting to be tapped into the order Bolt should do them.

images.concept: Turn each plan line into blocks
images.alt: The finished program for the plan level fills the tray: twenty-one blocks that follow the plan lines in order.

images.concept: Worked example: counting gems
images.alt: Halfway up the gem column, Bolt's counter pill reads count = 2: two gems picked up, two counted, and the change block is lit.

images.concept: The counting door
images.alt: Bolt's row holds three gems, then a door, then the flag; the door's counter reads count = 3 and the starter program counts.

images.concept: A named box
images.alt: The program names its box: set count to 0, then repeat 5 times move, pick up, and change count by 1, beside the gem column.

images.concept: Set and change
images.alt: Bolt stands by the door with the counter strip reading steps = 2: set steps to 4 started it, and change steps by -1 ticks it down.

images.concept: Hold a value (the starter names it x)
images.alt: The starter program counts with a box named x: set x to 0, change x by 1. The value works, but the name says nothing.

images.concept: Names are for people
images.alt: The same counting program with the box named count: set count to 0 and change count by 1 read like a sentence.

images.concept: Kinds of values
images.alt: A flag variable in the tray: set hasKey to Off at the start, and set hasKey to On inside the if block that picks the key up.

images.concept: Watch the value
images.alt: Two rounds into repeat 6, the watch strip reads steps = 4: set steps to 6 started it, and each change steps by -1 brings it down.

images.concept: the boss round
images.alt: Trick Inbox, the Boss Round: a stranger's game chat waits in the inbox, one clue found in green and one still hiding.

images.concept: a stranger in game chat
images.alt: Game chat from a player nobody knows: keep our chat secret from your parents, and a plan to meet. Both clues found.

images.concept: show Pim, the debrief
images.alt: The stranger's chat, shown to Pim: chat is for people you know in real life, so show a trusted adult.

images.concept: safe to deliver
images.alt: Mia's message, delivered: safe, because Mia is someone you know in real life and she asks for nothing.

images.concept: a kind chat from a classmate
images.alt: Game chat from Mia from Class: great game, your tower was amazing, see you at school tomorrow.

images.concept: a mean message
images.alt: Game chat from JokerJay: everyone laugh at Pip, and share this so the whole school sees.

images.concept: the mean message, the debrief
images.alt: The mean message, reported: do not join in, a kind word to Pip helps more, and save it and tell an adult.

images.concept: a free gift and a secret
images.alt: Game chat from NewFriend: a rare game skin, free, if you keep it our secret and send your game key.

images.concept: choosing the move in chat
images.alt: NewFriend's chat with both clues found, and the four moves below it: Deliver, Bin it, Show Pim, Report and block.

images.concept: a quiz that collects private facts
images.alt: A Fun Quiz in game chat asks for your first pet, the street you grew up on and your birthday.

images.concept: show Pim, the debrief
images.alt: A stranger's game chat, shown to Pim: someone who asks for secrets from adults and wants to meet is the biggest red flag.

images.concept: a mean message with an audience
images.alt: Game chat from JokerJay: everyone laugh at Pip, and share this so the whole school sees.

images.concept: the bystander move
images.alt: The mean message, reported: do not join in, never pass it on, and a kind word to Pip helps more than any reply.

images.concept: an online-only friend
images.alt: Game chat from NewFriend: you seem nice, a rare game skin for free, just keep this our secret.

images.concept: leaving is a move
images.alt: NewFriend's chat with both clues found, and the four moves below: Deliver, Bin it, Show Pim, Report and block.

images.concept: friendly questions that collect facts
images.alt: A Fun Quiz in game chat asks for your first pet, the street you grew up on and your birthday, then a share.

images.concept: a group chat dare
images.alt: Group chat: everyone is doing it, post the photo or you are out, and do not show any adult this chat.

images.concept: pressure, the debrief
images.alt: The group chat dare, reported: pressure dressed up as friendship, and leaving a chat like that is a strength.

images.concept: the prize letter, every clue found
images.alt: The tablet letter with all three clues found: you are our lucky winner, mailbox key, in the next ten minutes.

images.concept: a faked Post Office letter
images.alt: A letter from the Post Office Team says your mailbox will close unless you send your mailbox key today.

images.concept: free coins, too good to be true
images.alt: A Game Shop letter offers a thousand free coins, but the offer ends in one hour. Both clues are found.

images.concept: free coins, the debrief
images.alt: The free coins letter, binned: Pim explains it was too good to be true, from the prize-faker.

images.concept: a package you never ordered
images.alt: A Package Service letter: we could not deliver your package, pay a small fee within two hours.

images.concept: a hoax that begs to be shared
images.alt: Trick Inbox, Fake or Fact?: a news flash says school closes forever with free candy for a year. Share before they delete this!

images.concept: the hoax, the debrief
images.alt: The school closing post, binned: real news does not beg to be shared, so check big stories first.

images.concept: an ad in a prize costume
images.alt: A Prize Ad says tap to claim your free phone, but only the first fifty people get one.

images.concept: an AI fake
images.alt: A video clip shows the mayor singing in a fountain, but his mouth moves after the words end.

images.concept: the AI fake, the debrief
images.alt: The fountain video, shown to Pim: some videos are made by computers to look real. Check a real news page first.

images.concept: real news
images.alt: Netville News: the library opens its new reading room on Saturday. Ordinary news, no prizes and no panic.

images.concept: a quiz that harvests answers
images.alt: A Which Dragon Are You quiz asks for your first pet, your mother's first name and your birthday.

images.concept: a chain letter
images.alt: Magpie Mix: a chain letter says pass it to ten friends and a shiny surprise will find you tonight.

images.concept: the forwarder
images.alt: The chain letter, binned: the debrief names the forwarder, who wants you to share the trick with everyone.

images.concept: the key-hunter
images.alt: A letter asking for your mailbox key, binned: the debrief names the key-hunter, who wants into your mailbox.

images.concept: fake news with candy on top
images.alt: A post from News Flash says school is closing forever with free candy for everyone, and begs you to tell everyone.

images.concept: the giggler
images.alt: The school closing post, binned: the debrief names the giggler, who wants a big reaction.

images.concept: visitor number 1000
images.alt: A Prize Team letter says you are visitor number 1000 and can claim a free games console.

images.concept: the prize-faker
images.alt: The visitor prize, binned: you did not enter anything, so you cannot have won. The prize-faker sent it.

images.concept: the account thief
images.alt: A letter asking for your mailbox key, binned: the debrief names the key-hunter, who wants into your mailbox.

images.concept: the giggler
images.alt: The school closing post, binned: the debrief names the giggler, who wants a big reaction and a crowd.

images.concept: the prize-faker
images.alt: The visitor 1000 prize, binned: the debrief names the prize-faker, who wants you to tap and type.

images.concept: authority and a rush
images.alt: Trick Inbox, Pressure: a letter says this is the head teacher speaking. Send your key before lunch, no questions.

images.concept: authority, the debrief
images.alt: The head teacher letter, reported: authority is a costume here, and do not ask questions is the loudest clue.

images.concept: fear and a countdown
images.alt: A System letter says your account will be deleted in one hour unless you send your key right now.

images.concept: flattery from a public profile
images.alt: A Fan Club post knows you love skateboards, your dog's name and your birthday, and asks for your key.

images.concept: the footprint, the debrief
images.alt: The Fan Club post, binned: everything it knew came from a public profile. Flattery built from your footprint.

images.concept: a dare that spends a friend
images.alt: Group chat from The Cool Group: post a silly photo of your friend or leave the group. Everyone will laugh.

images.concept: a countdown hook
images.alt: A Shop Bot letter: only two left at this price, pay in the next five minutes or lose them forever.

images.concept: a faked sender, every clue found
images.alt: The faked Post Office letter with every clue found: the real address, the key ask, the rush, and a button that goes elsewhere.

images.concept: spoofing, the debrief
images.alt: The faked Post Office letter, reported: the name says Post Office, but the address and the button tell the truth.

images.concept: a faked sender, before the hunt
images.alt: Trick Inbox, Faked Senders: a letter from Post Office says your key expired. Its real address is a freemail box.

images.concept: a teacher in costume
images.alt: A letter named Your Teacher, sent from a stranger's mail box, asks where you live and for your mailbox key.

images.concept: Write a credit line / share or keep: weigh both sides before sharing
images.alt: A Would You Rather online dilemma: something you made, and the choice of whether to share it or keep it.

images.concept: Public or private? Public gets you seen, private keeps you safe
images.alt: An online dilemma in Pro: make it public and be found, or keep it private and stay safe — a real tradeoff.

images.concept: Post your art? Benefit: feedback. Risk: a logo shows where you are
images.alt: A second online dilemma: posting your work brings feedback, and can also show more than you meant.

images.concept: photos on your tablet, or a copy elsewhere
images.alt: Would you rather keep photos only on your own tablet, or keep a copy on a service someone else runs?

images.concept: a page anyone can comment on
images.alt: Would you rather put class work on a page anyone can comment on, or a page only your class can see?

images.concept: credit a picture, or draw your own
images.alt: Would you rather use a picture someone else made and credit them, or draw your own from scratch?

images.concept: delete an old post, or leave it
images.alt: Would you rather delete an old post you are embarrassed by, or leave it up and laugh about it?

images.concept: delete an old post, or leave it
images.alt: Would you rather delete an old post you are embarrassed by, or leave it up and laugh about it?

images.concept: ask before every download
images.alt: Would you rather ask a trusted adult before every download, or never download anything at all?

images.concept: a drawing for everyone, or family only
images.alt: Would you rather share a drawing so everyone can see it, or show it only to your family?

images.concept: a free game that sees where you are
images.alt: Would you rather play a free game that always sees where you are, or pay for one that never knows?

images.concept: nickname or real first name
images.alt: Would you rather use a nickname nobody can trace to you, or your real first name so friends can find you?

images.concept: nickname or real first name
images.alt: Would you rather use a nickname nobody can trace to you, or your real first name so friends can find you?

images.concept: What is technology? Anything people invent to solve a problem
images.alt: A Would You Rather technology dilemma: two inventions to choose between, and reasons to weigh on both sides.

images.concept: Tech changes how we live: every invention changes something else
images.alt: A second technology dilemma: a new choice about how an invention changes the way people live.

images.concept: Tradeoffs everywhere: a benefit for someone, a cost for someone else
images.alt: A Pro technology dilemma: each side of the choice helps someone and costs someone else.

images.concept: Automation: a machine does a task people used to do
images.alt: Another technology dilemma, about machines doing tasks people used to do, and what changes when they do.
